name: Venetian Red
lede: Venetian red is a warm brick-to-orange red iron oxide, named for Venice, that began as a natural earth and by the eighteenth century was largely a factory product made by heating iron sulfate with lime.

sections.title: Which Venetian red
sections.body:
*Venetian red* names a pigment first and a screen color second [1][13]. The pigment is a red iron oxide, the same compound, ferric oxide, that colors red ochre and rust [3][7]. The swatch on this page is the dictionary color: a deep reddish orange in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, dated to 1753 by Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary, and matched by a color within two units in the RAL industrial series, Traffic Red [14].

That swatch is bright and saturated, with a CIELCH chroma of about 82 [14]. The pigment's own color is not fixed. In the factory process the shade depends on the size of the particles that form during successive heating steps [4]. Treat the swatch as a name tag for a family of reds, not as a measurement of the paint [4][14].

sections.title: A red iron oxide
sections.body:
Chemically the pigment is iron(III) oxide of the hematite type, the mineral that gives red ochre its color [3][7]. Red ochres form where iron-rich rocks weather, with hematite spread through the earth as extremely fine grains [7]. The Romans called the common ones *rubrica*, the source of the English word rubric, and the Greeks *miltos* [7]. Pliny, Vitruvius and Theophrastus all discuss them, and the best was imported from Anatolia, from the port of Sinope, which gave its name to the finest, *sinopia* [7].

Red earth was in use long before anyone named it for Venice [7]. Ochre workings about 11,000 years old have been detected in eastern Wyoming [7], and one study suggests that heating ochre to turn it red was understood as far back as the Palaeolithic [3]. Pliny, writing in 77 AD, already mentions burnt ochres, and says they were adulterated with red lead in a mixture he calls *sandyx* [3].

sections.title: Venice, Verona or neither
sections.body:
Where the name came from is less settled than it looks. The Pigment Compendium reports that Venetian red was reputed to have first belonged to a natural red ochre from a deposit near Venice that has since been exhausted [2]. It cites Harley (1982) for the later move, and Merrifield (1849) places the original source at Verona instead [2]. When the real earth ran out, the name passed to a synthetic pigment because the manufactured color reproduced the old one [2]. The word *reputed* matters here: this is a tradition, not a documented fact [2].

Books disagree about what the name means today. Paterson defines it as a natural orange-red or reddish-brown iron oxide, known by many names according to the places where it is found [13]. Jarman likewise calls it a natural iron oxide, a warm ground for painters in Venice [11]. The Pigment Compendium, citing Church (1901), says that by then the name had moved to an artificial oxide made by calcining green vitriol [1]. The chemistry is the same iron oxide either way, and what differs is how it was made and how fine the grains are [3].

The books here do not say when the name first appeared in English [14]. Maerz and Paul date the color name to 1753 [14], and Chambers's *Cyclopaedia* was already discussing its neighbor Indian red in 1738 [6].

sections.title: Made from green vitriol
sections.body:
The factory method is the best-documented part of the story. Green vitriol, or copperas, is hydrated iron(II) sulfate [3]. Heated, it loses water, then sulfur trioxide, and leaves an iron oxide whose color depends on the size of the particles that form [4]. The compendium says the most accepted recipe for Venetian red was to calcine copperas with lime, and Fuller (1973) specifies copperas red, an oxide already made by heating iron sulfate, calcined with hydrated lime [3][1].

The compendium dates the product to the eighteenth century and calls it the first synthetic iron oxide made by any method other than roasting yellow ochres [3]. A manufactured oxide has a practical edge: its grains can be finer than a natural earth's, which gives a more transparent paint [3]. The compendium adds that this technology has only been available since the seventeenth century [3].

Copperas was cheap and had other uses, among them writing ink and dyeing [4]. Harley is cited for the idea that the related pigment *caput mortuum* arose as a by-product of making sulfuric acid in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, probably through an early form of the copperas process [5]. By 1973 Fuller found Venetian red neither popular nor economical to produce [1].

sections.title: A family of reds with tangled names
sections.body:
Venetian red is one of a crowd. The compendium lists Indian red, Tuscan red, Pompeian red, light red, rouge, terra Pozzuoli, crocus, colcothar and caput mortuum among terms generally applied to synthetic reds, and notes that the same words were used for natural and artificial versions alike, mostly to describe the shade [2]. Salter (1869) gives English red, Prussian red and scarlet ochre as equivalent names, and says Spanish red differed little [1]. Zerr and Rübencamp (1906) treat Venetian red as a synonym for [[indian-red]] [1].

The Indian red story shows how slippery the words were [6]. Chambers's *Cyclopaedia* (1738) calls it a purple ochre shipped from Ormus, an island in the Persian Gulf, but Dossie (1764) already observed that the color sold under the name was made from caput mortuum [6]. Ure (1875-78) likewise called it an earth first obtained from the East Indies and, by his day, prepared artificially by roasting iron sulfate [6]. Church (1901) separated the two by tint: the original Venetian red was less purplish than Indian red [1].

Place names do the rest. Paterson lists Persian red as a purplish red pigment and [[pompeian-red]] as the red of the Pompeii frescoes, both sending the reader to Venetian red, and gives Spanish ferreto as a reddish-brown pigment [13]. Fairholt (1854) is cited for [[spanish-red]] as an ochre resembling Venetian red but slightly yellower [8]. Weber (1923) describes [[tuscan-red]] and Pompeian red as iron oxide mixed with alizarin madder [2].

Even [[light-red]] is slippery. It is commonly applied to burnt yellow ochres, and Ibbetson (1803) distinguished a light red made from calcined green vitriol, which he says was called Venetian red, from one made by calcining yellow ochre, which he preferred [3][8]. The Italian *terra rosa* is linked by Mayer (1991) only with Venetian red, while Church thought its pinkish-red hue came from ferric oxide and that it was probably often, if not always, artificial [8]. The old term colcothar, from the early seventeenth century, is listed by Church as a synthetic red iron oxide synonymous with Venetian red, and Heaton (1928) treated it as nearly obsolete [5].

sections.title: A grey that shared the name
sections.body: A fifteenth-century recipe, copied by Merrifield (1849), uses the words *Venetian red* beside a different term, *veneda*, but the recipe it gives is for a grey: black mixed with white lead or lime [8]. Theophilus, writing in the twelfth century, recommends veneda for painting eyes [8]. The compendium files veneda under grey, and the books do not settle whether the two words are related [8]. It is a useful reminder that a color name in an old recipe may not mean the color we expect.

sections.title: In the studio
sections.body:
Ball repeats a remark sometimes attributed to [[painter:titian|Titian]]: use Venetian red, an earth color, but make it look like [[vermilion]] [9]. He gives it while discussing how Titian's later work builds a continuous, harmonious tonality, a style known as tonal painting [9]. The attribution is hedged in the source, so treat it as a studio saying rather than a documented statement [9].

Gurney, a modern painter and teacher, treats the color as a working tool. A thin transparent layer of Venetian red or burnt sienna laid on the panel first gives a warm base, and blues and greens sparkle by complementary contrast where it shows through [10]. In his sample palettes he lists Venetian red under the pigment code PR 101 [10]. By his account the figure palette of the old masters, from Rembrandt to Anders Zorn, was roughly white, yellow ochre, a red earth and black [10].

A limited palette of ultramarine blue, Venetian red and yellow ochre gives a narrow gamut, because the red and yellow sit close together on the color wheel [10]. Westland shows the same palette in a Gurney painting and notes how hard it is to mix a vivid purple from primaries chosen this way [12]. Jarman's short entry says that today the color is used more as a rust-resistant paint than as an artists' pigment [11].

sections.title: Mountbatten pink
sections.body: One of the oddest uses of the name came in 1940 [15]. Lord Mountbatten noticed that a requisitioned Union-Castle liner, still in its dull pinkish civilian paint, disappeared into the dusk well before the other ships in the convoy [15]. Soon the destroyers of his flotilla were painted a medium grey with a dash of Venetian red, a tone that became known as [[mountbatten-pink]] [15]. HMS Kenya, nicknamed the Pink Lady, survived heavy fire off Vaagso in late 1941 with only cosmetic damage, which some took as proof [15]. It is not known whether the Admiralty ever tested the color, and it was being phased out by 1942 [15].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 museum paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 45 works, about 0.2 per cent [16]. It is most concentrated in the 1400s, where 8 of 945 works match, roughly four and a half times the archive rate [16]. The earliest by date is [[painting:rijks-20026322|a Sienese painting of 1440]], where the color fills about a fifth of the picture [16]. [[painting:nga-46025|Portrait of a Man]], dated 1450, and two cardinals' portraits, of 1801 and [[painting:commons-Q59859476|A Cardinal]] of 1880, hold it over about a quarter of the canvas [16].

Among our named colors, [[brick]] shares paintings with it far more than chance would give, a lift of 14.7 across 28 works [16]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, and a color match is not a pigment test, so a match here cannot say whether iron oxide was used [16].

questions.q: Which description of the Venetian red of the 1700s is closest to the books?
choices: A synthetic iron oxide made by calcining copperas with lime
A mercury sulfide ground from cinnabar
A lake dyed from madder root
A copper green roasted from malachite
questions.answer: A synthetic iron oxide made by calcining copperas with lime

questions.q: True or false: the books agree that Venetian red has always been a natural earth dug near Venice.
What was added to a medium grey to make Mountbatten pink?

openers: Venetian red may never have been a Venetian mineral for most of its life: by the eighteenth century it was made by roasting green vitriol with lime.
Mountbatten pink, the Royal Navy's 1940 camouflage, was a medium grey with a dash of Venetian red.
Where to look: a warm Venetian-red ground showing through thin blue or green paint makes the blue or green seem to sparkle.

issues: Origin of the name rests on Harley (1982) and Merrifield (1849) as reported in the Pigment Compendium; marked as reputed.
Books disagree on natural vs. synthetic: Paterson and Jarman say natural oxide; Pigment Compendium (Church 1901, Fuller 1973) say artificial.
Swatch is bright (chroma 82); pigment color depends on particle size. Say so in the article.
Veneda link to Venetian red not established; stated as unresolved.
